analysis.one_liner: Requires the Pentagon and other defense agencies to obey the same environmental and public-health laws as everyone else.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 107th Congress and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the special exemptions that let the Department of Defense and other defense-related agencies, including the Department of Energy and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, operate outside federal and state environmental laws. It would waive the government's legal immunity so the Pentagon could be fined, ordered to clean up, or sued by citizens the same way a private company can be. It would also require environmental review for weapons development and repeal rules that blocked defense funds from paying environmental fines. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to six committees and a string of subcommittees and never received any hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near military installations and Department of Energy nuclear sites, base civilian workers, service members, and communities exposed to military pollution. The bill's text names children, members of the armed forces, civilian employees, and neighbors of military operations as the people it aims to protect. Residents would gain a new right to sue a polluting defense agency in federal court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near military installations and defense sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Defense and other federal defense agencies to comply with federal and state environmental and public-health laws to the same extent as any private entity, and expressly waives their sovereign immunity.

Creates a citizen-suit right, letting any person go to federal court to stop a defense agency's violation of an environmental permit, standard, or order, with attorneys' fees available to the prevailing party.
Repeals the federal provision that barred using military appropriation accounts to pay environmental fines and penalties, so noncompliance would carry a real financial consequence.
Extends coverage to Department of Energy and nuclear defense operations and to installations located outside the United States, closing gaps where defense pollution fell outside normal enforcement.
Requires the Secretary of Defense to ensure all weapon-system development and procurement decisions comply with the National Environmental Policy Act.

analysis.who_pays: The Department of Defense, Department of Energy, and other defense agencies would bear permit fees, fines, cleanup costs, and compliance spending drawn from the defense budget — costs ultimately funded by taxpayers, along with any constraints on training or operations needed to meet pollution standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Pentagon and the defense budget

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be expensive: the bill makes defense agencies liable for fines, penalties, permit fees, and service charges under a long list of laws including the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Superfund, and OSHA, with costs paid from defense appropriations that taxpayers fund.

Coverage of laws such as the Marine Mammal Protection Act, Noise Control Act, and Endangered Species Act — and of operations both inside and outside the United States — could constrain live-fire training, naval exercises, and overseas operations, raising genuine readiness and foreign-policy questions supporters would have had to answer.
Citizen suits with fee-shifting could invite litigation against defense installations, adding court battles on top of regulatory enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities living next to military pollution — the bill's own stated focus — the benefit of enforceable standards, fines, and a right to sue is substantial and the compliance cost is one every private polluter already bears. The honest counterweight is real: readiness constraints on training and the cost of cleanup are significant, and the blanket coverage of overseas operations was drafted broadly. On balance the bill asked the military to meet the same legal bar as everyone subject to the same laws.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees and then bounced among at least seven subcommittees, got an executive comment request from DOD and DOE six months in, and never reached a hearing or vote before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the Military Environmental Responsibility Act on June 13, 2001, joined by four original cosponsors including Reps. McKinney, Pelosi, DeGette, and Lewis of Georgia.
Twelve House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

The Speaker referred it to six committees — Armed Services, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Resources, Education and the Workforce, and Judiciary — which then sent pieces of it to seven different subcommittees.

Six months after introduction, in December 2001, the House requested executive comment from the Department of Defense and Department of Energy and referred the bill to the Armed Services Subcommittee on Military Readiness; that was the last action ever taken.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Department of Defense and other defense-related agencies kept their existing exemptions from environmental enforcement, continuing to operate without the fines, permit fees, and citizen lawsuits this bill would have allowed. Neighbors of military installations gained nothing.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Chairman Bob Stump

against.name: House Republican leadership

against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to six committees and a series of subcommittees where it could be shelved, and never scheduled it for floor action in two and a half years.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no vote was ever taken to test where the full chamber stood.

industries.industry: Department of Defense and defense-related agencies
industries.note: The bill would strip these agencies' exemptions from federal and state environmental laws, exposing them to fines, permit fees, cleanup orders, and citizen suits the way private polluters are. Their interest in staying exempt runs directly against the health of people living near their installations, and their success in avoiding a vote preserved that exemption.

The bill would require environmental review of all weapon-system development and procurement decisions, adding compliance steps to programs contractors build. The burden is modest but real, and contractors' interest in unreviewed procurement runs against the communities affected by weapons production and testing.
